Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :

Titre d'origine : The macroeconomic effects of defence spending: what impact beyond GDP?

ARTICLE :
Working Paper Series 
The macroeconomic effects of 
defence spending: what impact 
beyond GDP? 
Cristina Checherita-Westphal, 
Laust L. Særkjær 
Disclaimer: This paper should not be reported as representing the views of the European Central Bank 
(ECB). The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect those of the ECB. 
No 3310 / November 2026 
Abstract
This paper estimates the macroeconomic effects of defence spending for a panel of up
to 27 EU member states over 1999–2025 using Panel Local Projections. We look beyond
the output multiplier that dominates the literature to trace the price implications of defence
spending and the demand-side channels through which effects operate. A key methodological
contribution is a country-specific order-date adjustment for capital expenditure, constructed
from the SIPRI Arms Transfers Database, which shifts the estimated (unitary) peak GDP
multiplier from around year one to approximately year three to four. Under this specifica-
tion, the HICP inflation response is higher and occurs earlier. Capital expenditure drives the
positive output effects, whereas personnel and intermediate consumption generate stronger
inflationary pressures per unit of fiscal impulse. Capital spending induces additional recur-
rent costs, standing at about 30 cents per euro spent over five years. Multipliers are also
found to be substantially lower, on average, in high public debt regimes.
Keywords:MilitaryExpenditure; FiscalMultiplier; LocalProjections; EuropeanUnion; Spend-
ing Composition
JEL Classification:E31, E62, H54, H56

Non-technical summary
European governments are rapidly increasing defence expenditure. Russia’s full-scale invasion of
Ukraine in February 2022 triggered immediate budgetary responses across EU member states,
and the European Commission’sReArm Europe Planinitiative from March 2025 has elevated
national and EU-wide defence ambitions to a structural priority. Understanding the macroeco-
nomic consequences of this fiscal shift has become a priority not only for defence planners and
fiscal authorities, but also for central banks: a sustained increase in public spending at this scale
can increase inflation, shift trade balances, and interact with existing fiscal vulnerabilities in
ways that go beyond real GDP.
This paper first provides a comprehensive empirical assessment of these macroeconomic ef-
fects, particularly inflation. We use a Panel Local Projection method, tracing how each variable
of interest – real GDP, price dynamics, household consumption, net exports, and private invest-
ment – responds over a five-year horizon to an increase in defence spending, providing a richer
picture of the fiscal transmission mechanism than estimates focused solely on output. Second,
since our focus lies on European-wide effects, we use data for 27 EU member states from 1999
(and earlier) until 2025, thus drawing on more than two decades of variation in defence spending,
while also providing an up-to-date EU assessment that covers the post-2022 build-up.
Finally, a central methodological contribution of our paper is the novel correction for a
recording lag in European national accounts (the COFOG database, which classifies government
expenditure by function). Under EU accounting rules, capital spending such as major weapons
systems is recorded atdelivery, not atorder. For equipment that is often delivered several years
after it is ordered, official data show a spending increase years after the actual fiscal decision.
Using the Arms Transfers Database of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute
(SIPRI), we construct country-specific order-date adjustments for all 27 EU member states, with
lagsrangingfromzeroyears(Malta)tofouryears(Germany, Italy, Sweden, andtheNetherlands).
Applying these adjustments shifts the estimated peak GDP response from year one to year three
to four. At the same time, the inflation effect is larger and kicks in earlier. These are important
differences for both budget planning and monetary policy assessment.
Turning to the size of estimates, a one percent of GDP increase in total defence spending
generates a GDP multiplier of approximately unity at its peak, consistent with the broader
government spending literature. Both multipliers lie below their respective peaks by the five-

year horizon – the unadjusted settling at around 0.3, the adjusted one higher, at around 0.6. On
the price side, consumer prices (HICP) and the GDP deflator rise persistently, with the deflator
response generally larger – reflecting that defence-specific cost pressures show up directly in
government deflators, while HICP effects operate through indirect channels. In the adjusted
specification, cumulative HICP inflation reaches about 1 percentage point by year one, peaks at
about 1.4 percentage points in year three and remains at around 1.25 percentage points at the
five-year horizon. The inflation effect also holds, with a smaller magnitude, when the sample
ends in 2021, before the inflation surge.
The aggregate figures, however, conceal substantial differences across spending categories.
Capital expenditure drives the GDP effects of defence spending, generating the largest and most
persistentoutputmultiplier. Personnelcostsandintermediateconsumption, bycontrast, produce
stronger inflationary pressure per euro of fiscal impulse but more limited output effects. Capital
procurement also generatesrecurrent costs: each additional euro triggers approximately 30 cents
of additional personnel and maintenance spending over five years, implying that the true fiscal
cost of a procurement-heavy build-up substantially exceeds the initial capital appropriation.
The macroeconomic returns to defence spending also depend on fiscal space. EU member
states differ widely in their public debt positions, and countries with high(er) public debt see
substantially lower multipliers, although these estimates are imprecise.
The baseline results for total defence spending are robust to alternative lag lengths, detrend-
ing methods, and monetary policy controls, as well as to GDP weighting, leave-one-out country
exclusion, winsorising outlier observations, excluding a small residual spending category, cor-
recting for military donations to Ukraine, and measuring defence spending with the SIPRI (as
opposed to COFOG) database. Yet, substantial uncertainty surrounds the estimates, in partic-
ular the size of GDP multipliers across various periods and country samples. For the past EU
defence spending in our sample, the statistical significance tends to be stronger for higher price
effects (mostly originating from personnel spending), negative net exports, and larger recurrent
(personnel and maintenance) costs of capital procurement.

1 Introduction
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, governments across the European
Union have announced, and in many cases implemented, substantial increases in military expen-
diture, driven both by direct security concerns and by NATO commitments to higher defence
targets. At the Hague summit in June 2025, NATO members agreed a new headline target of
5% of GDP by 2035, comprising at least 3.5% for core defence requirements and up to 1.5%
for defence- and security-related investment such as infrastructure and industrial capacity. In
parallel, the European Commission’sReArm Europe Plan, announced in March 2025, and the
subsequent activation over the period 2025-28 of the national escape clause under the reformed
EU fiscal framework have opened fiscal space for member states to act on these commitments.
Policymakers, fiscal authorities and central banks therefore need to understand the macroeco-
nomiceffectsofdefenceexpenditure, onpricesaswellasonoutput, andthedemand-sidechannels
through which they operate.
The empirical literature on defence spending multipliers has predominantly focused on the
United States, where large military buildups provide sharp and plausibly exogenous variation
in government spending (Ramey and Shapiro, 1998; Ramey, 2011; Ramey and Zubairy, 2018).
European evidence is more limited, but EU-specific estimates are emerging strongly. More fun-
damentally, the literature has focused almost exclusively on the real GDP response, leaving the
inflationary consequences of defence spending far less studied.1 This is a significant gap: from
the perspective of monetary policy, the price effects of a large and sustained fiscal expansion in
defence matter at least as much as the output effects.
The methodological backbone of the defence spending multiplier literature traces to Barro
(1981)andreceivednewimpetuswiththenarrativeidentificationapproachofRameyandShapiro
(1998), who exploit US military buildups as quasi-exogenous variation in government spending.
Ramey and Zubairy (2018) combine the local projection method of Jordà (2005) with narrative
shock identification and cumulative multiplier definitions, providing a comprehensive treatment
of US government spending multipliers, including in periods of economic slack and near the zero
lower bound. These contributions form the basis for our empirical approach.
1Price responses do feature in some recent work. For the EU27 sample, Furceri et al. (2026) find that consumer
prices rise (shown in their figure 7), and Alloza et al. (2026) report price responses alongside GDP components
for Spain, but these are typically a secondary result rather than an object of study, and we are not aware of a
systematic investigation of price effects, including by spending category.

4
Fordefencespendingspecifically, thecross-countrypanelevidenceinSheremirovandSpirovska
(2022) covers a broad sample of advanced and developing economies and finds multipliers in ad-
vanced economies roughly twice those in developing ones. More generally, state dependence
in government spending multipliers has been studied by, among others, Auerbach and Gorod-
nichenko (2012), who find larger multipliers in times of economic slack, and Nickel and Tudyka
(2014), who find that high public debt attenuates them. We adapt their empirical specifications
for our debt-state analysis.
EU-specific evidence is expanding rapidly. García Serrador et al. (2025) estimate defence
spending multipliers for the EU27 using local projections, with particular attention to spending
composition and non-linearities across fiscal space and other regimes. Olejnik (2023) examines
multipliers for NATO’s eastern-flank countries over 1999–2021. For Spain, Alloza et al. (2026)
construct a comprehensive series of defence procurement contracts timed at order placement
rather than delivery, directly highlighting the timing problem we address systematically for all
EU member states through the order-date adjustment. Most recently, two IMF contributions
have analysed the topic. Furceri et al. (2026) use procurement data to estimate cumulative GDP
multipliers ranging from around 1.3 at impact to close to 2 at the two-year horizon for a panel of
EU27 countries, with multipliers larger where import intensity is low and fiscal space is ample.
The April 2026 World Economic Outlook devotes a chapter to defence spending (International
Monetary Fund, 2026), drawing on data for 164 countries since 1946. Following a peacetime
defence spending boom, real output is more than 3% higher than in periods without a boom,
with the gain materialising about two years after onset, and defence spending multipliers are close
to 1 on average. Restricting the sample to NATO members gives similar, though less precisely
estimated, multipliers, and model simulations calibrated to the planned EU build-up yield a
medium-term multiplier of about 0.8. Appendix A.1 brings these and other US, cross-country
and EU estimates together in a single figure, at short and medium horizons. They range from
about zero to above two, with a median close to one, in line with our peak estimates.
Our central contribution to this literature is methodological. Under the European System of
Accounts 2010 (ESA 2010), defence capital goods are recorded in national accounts at the time
of delivery, not at the time of order. Major weapons systems, such as aircraft, naval vessels and
armoured vehicles, are often delivered several years after they are ordered, creating a systematic
misalignment between the timing of the fiscal decision and its appearance in the data. We address
this by constructing country-specific order-date adjustments using the SIPRI Arms Transfers
ECB Working Paper Series No 3310
5
Database (ATDB; Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, 2025), which records both
order and delivery dates for all international transfers of major conventional weapons. Another
contribution is to trace the macroeconomic effects of defence spending beyond output, particu-
larly on inflation, and to do so separately for capital expenditure, personnel and intermediate
consumption. We examine the demand-side channels through which these effects operate and
document the recurrent costs that capital acquisitions induce. In line with other studies, we also
estimate state-dependent multipliers, using government debt as a proxy for fiscal space.
Finally, our analysis covers up to 27 EU member states over 1999–2025, using Eurostat’s
Classification of the Functions of Government (COFOG). It thus includes the post-2022 build-
up so far, providing an up-to-date EU-wide assessment. This matters because the build-up is
fast by historical standards: in real terms, EU defence spending rose by about 10 per cent in
2024 alone, more than in any earlier year of our sample, and announced plans point to further
increases.
Our main results are as follows. Aggregate defence spending generates a cumulative GDP
multiplier of around unity at its peak, with the adjusted specification peaking later than the
unadjusted one. Price effects are positive and significant, with GDP deflator growth generally
rising more than HICP inflation. Capital expenditure is the primary source of GDP gains (but
it also generates recurrent costs); personnel and intermediate consumption generate relatively
stronger price effects per euro spent. Household consumption rises and net exports deteriorate,
particularly in reaction to personnel and intermediate consumption spending. Fiscal space con-
ditions the estimates: on average, high-debt countries see smaller output and price responses
from increased defence spending.
The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 describes the data, including
the construction of the order-date adjustment. Section 3 presents the empirical model. Section 4
presents the results, encompassing the baseline impulse responses, the sub-category decompo-
sition, the fiscal implications of capital procurement, and the debt-state analysis. Section 5
concludes.
2 Data
Three public sources measure defence spending for EU countries with sufficient historical depth:
Eurostat’s Classification of the Functions of Government (COFOG), the Stockholm International
ECB Working Paper Series No 3310
6
Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), and NATO. We take COFOG as our baseline for two reasons.
First, it is compiled under the European System of Accounts (ESA 2010), so it is measured on
a consistent methodology across all 27 member states and is directly comparable with GDP and
its components. Second, COFOG provides an economic decomposition of defence spending into
gross fixed capital formation, compensation of employees, and intermediate consumption, on
the same national-accounts definitions as the outcome variables, which underpins the spending-
composition analysis at the heart of the paper.
All macroeconomic and fiscal data are drawn from Eurostat, with additional macro-financial
series (e.g., short- and long-term nominal interest rates) taken mostly from AMECO and used
only in robustness specifications. The estimation panel covers up to 27 EU member states over
1995–2025; for the 1999-start baseline it is close to balanced, the one material exception being
Slovakia, whose COFOG defence series begins only in 2010. The dependent variable and the
control set are described together with the empirical model in Section 3.

2.2 Composition of EU Defence Expenditure
Figure 2 plots the composition of EU27 aggregate defence spending over 1995–2024 based on
COFOG data. Personnel costs have consistently been the dominant component, accounting for
roughly half of total spending over most of the sample. Intermediate consumption (operations
and maintenance, such as fuel, spare parts and contracted services) represents approximately
one quarter. Gross fixed capital formation, which includes the weapon systems and platforms
that ESA 2010 classifies as fixed assets, such as warships, aircraft and armoured vehicles, has
remained broadly stable at around one fifth throughout the period.3 A residual category, mainly
current transfers such as contributions to international organisations before 2022 and investment
grants largely related to military aid since then, has been small historically (about 3 per cent
of total spending over 1999–2021) but has grown markedly since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine
(about 9 per cent over 2022–2024).4

2.3 Order-Date Adjustment for Capital Expenditure
UnderESA2010, militaryweaponsystemsareclassifiedasfixedassetsandrecordedasgrossfixed
capital formation at the time of delivery, not at the time of order (Eurostat, 2013, paras. 20.190–
20.191). Delivery is taken to occur when the military forces take possession of the equipment,
and for heavy equipment that takes many years to build, such as large ships or submarines, the
unfinished good remains work in progress in the producer’s inventories, so no government expen-
diture is recorded while it is under construction (Eurostat, 2016, Section II.5). The progressive
recording that applies to uncompleted buildings is explicitly not extended to such assets. The
gap between fiscal decision and national accounts recording can therefore span several years; in
the ATDB used below, for instance, the median time from order to delivery is three years for
tanks and frigates and six years for submarines. This timing mismatch matters for local pro-
jections: the measured capital spending at timet partly reflects order decisions madek years
earlier, where k is the delivery lag, and treating delivery-date recording as the timing of the
impulse will attribute output effects to the wrong period.

4.4 State Dependence and Fiscal Space
The macroeconomic effectiveness of fiscal policy may depend on prevailing conditions. A dimen-
sion of particular relevance for the current EU context is the level of government indebtedness.
High-debt and deficit countries face tighter constraints, such as higher borrowing costs, greater
Ricardian anticipation of future consolidation by forward-looking households, and reduced policy
credibility (Checherita-Westphal and Rother, 2012). The fiscal multiplier literature documents
that high public debt levels attenuate multipliers (Nickel and Tudyka, 2014; Kirchner et al.,
2010). Fiscal positions across EU member states are highly heterogeneous, and the fiscal space
available to finance defence investment varies widely.

with γ = 1.5, where zi,t−1 is the standardised lagged debt-to-GDP ratio, so that the weight rises
smoothly with indebtedness.

In the low-debt state, the GDP multiplier is positive throughout and peaks at about 2.6

state until year three, consistent with the Ricardian channel discussed above. As a robustness
check, we also define the high-debt state by discrete thresholds, as a lagged debt ratio above 60 or
90 per cent of GDP; these variants deliver a similar message in years one to three (Appendix A.4).

4.5 Robustness
The core results are overall robust across several dimensions, as documented in Appendix A.5.
SIPRI data.SIPRI total defence spending is an independently constructed series built on
a broader, cash-based perimeter. Re-estimating on it yields a GDP multiplier profile close to the
COFOG baseline, though lower at the peak (about 0.7 against 1.1) (Figure A.5.1). The price
responses remain statistically significant, positive and persistent, but their composition differs:
under SIPRI the HICP response reaches approximately 1.1 percentage points and exceeds the
deflator response. This most likely reflects SIPRI’s broader coverage of defence-related spending
outside the COFOG boundary, military pensions in particular, whose price effects fall relatively
more on consumer prices than on the government-output deflator. The finding of material price
effects is therefore robust to the choice of measure, while their incidence across the two price
gauges depends on the spending perimeter.
Lag order.Re-estimating with two and three lags rather than the baseline four produces
closely tracking impulse responses for both total and adjusted total defence (Figure A.5.2),
confirming that results do not depend on the particular lag length chosen.
Detrending and normalisation.The baseline fifth-order polynomial detrend is compared
against fourth- and sixth-order alternatives, as well as contemporaneous trend GDP and lagged
actual GDP normalisation (Figure A.5.3). In 2 out of 4 alternatives, GDP multipliers are larger,
while price effects are broadly unchanged. Apart from the small and insignificant private invest-
ment response, no variable changes sign. The relatively close agreement across all four variants
and the baseline confirms that results are not driven by a particular detrending choice.
Monetary and financial conditions vs. time fixed effects. The baseline relies on
year fixed effects to absorb common monetary policy variation. Replacing or augmenting these
with shadow interest rate measures (Wu and Xia, 2016; Lemke and Vladu, 2017) or long- and
short-term nominal interest rates leaves the sign and shape of the responses unchanged, with
the specifications that retain year fixed effects sitting somewhat below those that replace them,
particularlyintheunadjusteddefencespendingspecification(FigureA.5.4). Allofthesevariants,
including the baseline reproduced for comparison, are estimated on the common sample for which
the interest rate series are available. That sample is shorter than the headline one and raises
the estimated GDP multiplier throughout, so the exercise is informative about the treatment of
common macroeconomic conditions rather than about the level of the multiplier.

Weighting. Baseline results are broadly replicated under GDP-weighted estimation, con-
firming that the findings are not mechanically driven by the equal-country weighting (Fig-
ure A.5.5). For inflation, such effects carry more relevance for the euro area common monetary
policy (covering most countries in the sample). In this specification, the GDP-weighted output
response builds more gradually, consistent with the longer procurement cycles of the largest
economies, but reaches a similar magnitude by the end of the horizon. The HICP responses are
close to the baseline, except that the response to total defence spending is somewhat higher in
years 4–5, whereas the deflator response is higher for total and lower for adjusted total defence
spending.
Outliers. Re-estimating on data winsorized at the pooled 1st and 99th percentiles produces
closely tracking impulse responses (Figure A.5.6), confirming that the estimates are not driven
by extreme observations.
Country sample sensitivity.A leave-one-out exercise re-estimates the baseline 27 times,
excluding one member state at a time, and compares the estimated responses at the baseline
peak horizon (Figure A.5.7). No single exclusion moves the estimated GDP, HICP inflation, or
deflator growth response outside the 68 per cent confidence band of the baseline, indicating that
the results are not driven by any individual country. Repeating the exercise for the effects of
adjusted capital defence spending identifies one exception (Figure A.5.8): excluding Latvia raises
both the private investment and the GDP response materially.
Composition effects. Excluding the small residual spending category, or correcting cap-
ital spending for military donations from existing stocks, which the order-date adjustment can
otherwise distort, leaves the GDP response to adjusted total defence spending virtually un-
changed. The HICP response remains statistically significant from year one, but not on impact
(Figure A.5.9).
Overall. Across these checks, which concern total and adjusted total defence spending, the
GDP and price responses keep their sign. The GDP multiplier does show some sensitivity to
specification, most visibly to the detrending and normalisation choice, which rescales the output
response. The price responses are broadly more stable.

5 Conclusions
This paper has estimated the macroeconomic effects of defence spending for the EU27, providing
a comprehensive analysis that extends beyond the traditional GDP multiplier focus. Three main
findings emerge.
First, the timing of the fiscal impulse matters. The order-date adjustment moves capital
defence spending from delivery-date to order-date timing, using country-specific procurement
lags from the SIPRI Arms Transfers Database. It shifts the estimated peak of the GDP multiplier
from approximately the first year under the unadjusted specification to year three or four under
the adjusted one. The level of the cumulative GDP multiplier at its peak is around unity in
both specifications, but the temporal profile differs, and the multiplier remains higher at the
five-year horizon under the adjustment (0.6 against 0.3), although the two estimates rest on
samples that end in different years (Section 4.1). On the price side, consumer prices (HICP)
and the GDP deflator rise persistently, with the deflator response generally larger, reflecting
that defence-specific cost pressures show up directly in government deflators, while HICP effects
operate more through indirect channels. The HICP inflation effect in the adjusted specification
occurs earlier and is higher at every horizon than in the unadjusted setting. It peaks at about
1.4 percentage points in year three and is robust from year one, including when the sample ends
in 2021, before the inflation surge, whereas the significant impact response is not. For both fiscal
planning and monetary policy assessment, the distinction between a near-term and a three-to-five
year response is substantively important.
Second, spending composition is decisive. Capital expenditure drives GDP effects while
personnel and intermediate consumption, particularly personnel, generate stronger inflationary
pressure per unit of fiscal impulse. Capital acquisition also induces persistent increases in main-
tenance and personnel costs of approximately 30 cents per euro over five years, implying that the
medium-term fiscal cost of procurement programmes may substantially exceed the initial invest-
ment outlay. The recurrent-cost implications of capital defence spending commitments should
be built into fiscal plans. To the extent that the current build-up is tilted towards capital spend-
ing, our estimates point to a larger output effect, albeit with a delay, and a smaller inflationary
impact per euro than the historical spending mix.
Third, fiscal space conditions the macroeconomic returns to defence spending, with high(er)-
debt EU member states exhibiting, ceteris paribus, lower GDP multipliers (and price increases)

than their low-debt counterparts, although these estimates are imprecise. The effect comes
mainly through household consumption, whose response is markedly weaker in high-debt coun-
tries.
The baseline responses to total and adjusted total defence spending survive a range of speci-
fication checks: alternative lag lengths and detrending choices, explicit controls for the monetary
policy stance and financial conditions, GDP weighting, the exclusion of individual member states,
winsorisation of extreme observations, the exclusion of the residual spending category and the
correction of capital spending for military donations. They also hold when defence spending is
measured with the SIPRI series rather than COFOG, where the HICP inflation response is larger
than the deflator growth response.
Several caveats apply. Our estimates reflect average historical relationships and may not fully
capture non-linearities arising from the unprecedented speed and scale of the current build-up,
including industrial capacity constraints, input price bottlenecks, and supply chain disruptions.
Relatedly, including the most recent observations lowers the estimated GDP multiplier at every
horizon; whether this reflects timing (consistent with a build-up whose output effects have not
yet materialised in the data) or genuinely smaller multipliers in the current episode cannot yet
be established. The analysis is based on the EU27 as a whole; country-level evidence would
complement the panel estimates. While we use country fixed effects throughout to control for
country-specificcharacteristics, adeeperanalysisofthelocationofmilitaryequipmentproduction
and its spillover effects would bring substantial value added, particularly for the GDP effects.
Finally, the interaction with monetary policy and specifically whether and how the output and
inflationary effects of defence spending-induced fiscal expansions depend on the monetary policy
reaction warrants further investigation.
